# Statement of Need

*Inline tags show which rubric points each passage satisfies. Placeholders are in [brackets].*

---

## Statement of Need

In Eastside, more than one in five adults cannot read well enough to complete a job application, follow a prescription label, or help a child with homework. **[Need: Clarity of problem]**

### The Scope of the Problem

Approximately 22% of Eastside adults read below a sixth-grade level [Source, Year], compared with [X]% citywide and [Y]% statewide [Source, Year]. That represents an estimated [number] residents age 18 and older [U.S. Census ACS, Year]. This gap is not new. In [baseline year], the rate was [Z]% [Source, Year], showing that the need has [persisted/grown] despite existing efforts. **[Need: Data, Trend]**

### Who Is Affected

Low literacy is concentrated among [working-age adults ages 25–54, parents of school-age children, English language learners, and residents without a high school diploma]. In Eastside, [X]% of adults over 25 lack a high school diploma or equivalent [ACS, Year], and [X]% of households live below the federal poverty line [ACS, Year], compared with [X]% citywide. **[Need: Target population, Data]**

### Why It Matters

Low literacy is a root barrier that compounds other hardships:

- **Employment:** Adults with low literacy skills are [X] times more likely to be unemployed and earn [X]% less than adults with proficient skills [National source, e.g., PIAAC/NCES, Year]. Eastside's unemployment rate of [X]% exceeds the city average of [X]% [Bureau of Labor Statistics/State Labor Dept., Year].
- **Health:** Limited literacy is linked to higher rates of hospitalization, medication errors, and missed preventive care [Source, Year].
- **Access to services:** Residents who cannot navigate written forms struggle to apply for benefits, housing, and legal protections they qualify for.
- **Intergenerational impact:** A parent's literacy level is one of the strongest predictors of a child's reading achievement [Source, Year]. Local schools report declining family engagement in adult programs [School District, Year], weakening a critical link between home and classroom. **[Need: Community impact]**

### The Service Gap

Demand far exceeds capacity. Currently, **120 adults are on the waiting list** for basic literacy classes, with an average wait of **six months** [Internal records, Month Year]. Only [number] providers offer adult basic literacy instruction in Eastside, with a combined capacity of [number] seats per year [Source/Provider survey, Year]. Every month, adults who have found the courage to ask for help are turned away, and [X]% of waitlisted adults do not return when a seat opens [Internal data, Year]. **[Need: Data, Clarity of problem]**

### Community Voice

Residents themselves have named this priority. In a 2025 community survey (n=184), adult education ranked among residents' top [three] concerns, with [X]% of respondents identifying it as a critical need [Organization Survey, 2025]. **[Need: Target population, Data]**

> **[Testimonial slot, 2–3 sentences]**
> *"[Quote describing a personal barrier caused by low literacy, e.g., a missed job, a child's homework, a medical form, and what learning to read would change.]"*
> — [First name or initials], Eastside resident, [age/role, e.g., parent of two]

### Why Now

[Local timing factor: e.g., new employers opening in the district that require basic certification, a citywide workforce initiative, or school district family-engagement goals.] Without expanded capacity, the waitlist will continue to grow and the gap will widen for the next generation. **[Need: Community impact]**

[Organization]'s proposed program responds directly to these needs by [one-line preview of program, e.g., doubling class capacity, eliminating the waitlist within 18 months, and pairing literacy instruction with workforce and family supports], as detailed in the following section.

---

*≈600 words, excluding tags.*

## Fill-In Checklist

| Placeholder | Likely Source |
|---|---|
| City/state literacy comparison | State adult education office; PIAAC U.S. Skills Map (county-level estimates) |
| Population, education, poverty | U.S. Census American Community Survey (5-year estimates) |
| Unemployment | BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics or state labor department |
| Employment/health impacts | NCES/PIAAC; health literacy research (AHRQ, CDC) |
| School engagement decline | School district report or a letter from a principal |
| Provider capacity | Your own scan of local providers (a short table works well) |
| Waitlist attrition | Your intake records |
| Survey breakdown | Your 2025 survey data |

**Two quick tips:**
- If a data point can't be found, cut the sentence rather than leave a vague claim. Reviewers score specificity.
- Choose a testimonial that names a *concrete* consequence (a lost job, an unreadable form). It will land harder than a general statement.

# Target Population

*Inline tags show which rubric points each passage satisfies. Placeholders are in [brackets].*

## Target Population

[Organization] will serve **[150] adults per year** ([300] over the two-year grant period) who live or work in Eastside and read below a sixth-grade level. This target clears the current waitlist of 120 adults in year one while absorbing new demand. **[Need: Target population, Data]**

### Eligibility and Verification

| Criterion | How We Verify |
|---|---|
| Age 18 or older and not enrolled in K–12 | Self-attestation at intake |
| Lives or works in Eastside ([ZIP codes]) | Address on any document (utility bill, pay stub, lease) or signed self-attestation |
| Reads below a sixth-grade level | Standardized placement assessment ([CASAS/TABE]) at intake |

We accept self-attestation for residency so that documentation barriers do not exclude the adults with the greatest need. **[Need: Target population, Clarity]**

### Who They Are

Based on Eastside data and our current waitlist, we expect participants to reflect the following profile:

- **Age:** [X]% ages 25–54, prime working years [Internal waitlist data, Year]
- **Education:** [X]% lack a high school diploma or equivalent [ACS, Year]
- **Income:** [X]% of households below the federal poverty line [ACS, Year]
- **Family:** [X]% are parents or caregivers of school-age children [Internal data, Year]
- **Language:** [X]% speak a language other than English at home [ACS, Year]
- **Race/ethnicity:** [Breakdown, if relevant to need] [ACS, Year]

**[Need: Target population, Data]**

### Outreach and Recruitment

We will enroll our existing waitlist first, then recruit through trusted community channels:

- **Schools:** Family liaisons at [number] Eastside schools refer parents.
- **Workforce partners:** [American Job Center/employers] refer job seekers who screen below basic literacy.
- **Health and social services:** [Clinic, food bank, housing agency] staff refer clients who struggle with forms.
- **Community anchors:** [Library branches, faith congregations] host sign-up days.

Outreach materials will use plain language and pictures, and staff will offer word-of-mouth and in-person enrollment rather than relying on written flyers. **[Need: Target population; Program Design: Logic]**

---

*≈300 words, excluding tags and table formatting.*

## Phrasing Hooks to Copy

1. "We will serve [number] adults annually, prioritizing the [120] residents currently on our waitlist, who have waited an average of six months for a seat."
2. "Because low-literacy adults rarely respond to written outreach, we recruit through the people they already trust: teachers, caseworkers, clinic staff, and faith leaders."
3. "Eligibility is confirmed through a standardized [CASAS/TABE] assessment at intake, ensuring services reach the adults with the greatest need."

## Quick Notes

- **Check the service number against your budget.** Your annual target should match staffing capacity in Section 5 and cost per participant in Section 8. Reviewers cross-check these numbers.

# Program Design & Activities

*Inline tags show which rubric points each passage satisfies. Placeholders are in [brackets].*

---

## Program Design & Activities

[Program Name] is a [two-year] adult literacy program that will move [150] Eastside adults per year from below a sixth-grade reading level toward functional literacy. It combines structured instruction, individualized tutoring, real-world skill application, and the practical supports adults need to keep attending. **[Program Design: Logic]**

### Logic Model Summary

Our theory of change is straightforward. Adults with low literacy face two kinds of barriers: **skill barriers** (they need instruction) and **participation barriers** (childcare, transportation, schedules, and stigma that prevent them from staying long enough to gain skills). Most programs address only the first. Ours addresses both.

**If** adults receive consistent, evidence-based instruction applied to their daily lives, **and** we remove the logistical barriers that cause dropout, **then** they will persist long enough to make measurable reading gains. **Those gains** will lead to stronger employment prospects, greater independence in navigating health and social services, and more active support for their children's learning. *(See Attachment [X]: Logic Model.)* **[Program Design: Logic; links to Need and Outcomes]**

### Participant Pathway

| Phase | Timing | What Happens |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Intake** | Week 0–1 | Eligibility check, [CASAS/TABE] placement assessment, goal-setting interview, barrier screening (childcare, transportation, schedule) |
| **2. Instruction** | Weeks 1–16 | Small-group classes, weekly tutoring, applied literacy modules, wraparound supports |
| **3. Exit** | Week 16 | Post-assessment, individual progress review, next-step plan (next level, GED prep, job training, or workforce referral) |
| **4. Follow-up** | 3 and 6 months post-exit | Check-in calls on employment, continued learning, and goal attainment |

Participants who need more time may re-enroll in the next cycle at their new level. **[Program Design: Logic, Timeline]**

### Core Activities

**1. Small-Group Literacy Instruction**
Cohorts of [12–15] adults meet **3 times per week for 2 hours** over a **16-week cycle** (~[96] instructional hours). Classes run [3–4] cohorts per cycle, three cycles per year, with morning and evening options. Instruction follows [curriculum, e.g., a structured phonics and fluency approach aligned to College and Career Readiness Standards for Adult Education]. Research indicates adults typically need [X–Y] instructional hours to advance one educational functioning level [Source, Year], so this dosage is designed to produce measurable gains within a single cycle.
*Staffing:* [2.0] FTE Literacy Instructors (certified in adult education). **[Program Design: Logic, Staffing]**

**2. One-on-One Tutoring**
Each participant is matched with a trained volunteer tutor for **1 hour per week**, reinforcing classroom skills and targeting individual gaps. Tutors complete [12] hours of training before matching.
*Staffing:* [0.5] FTE Volunteer Coordinator recruits, trains, and supervises [40–50] tutors. **[Program Design: Staffing]**

**3. Applied Literacy Modules**
Classes include **biweekly modules** that apply reading skills to real tasks: job applications and workplace documents, health forms and prescription labels, benefits applications, and children's homework and school communications. Instruction tied to learners' own goals improves both persistence and skill transfer [Source, Year].
*Staffing:* Delivered by instructors, with guest sessions from [workforce and health partners]. **[Program Design: Logic; links to Need]**

**4. Family Literacy Nights**
**Monthly** evening sessions bring parents and children together for shared reading and school-readiness activities, held in partnership with [number] Eastside schools. This activity directly addresses the decline in family engagement reported by local schools.
*Staffing:* Instructors and school family liaisons. **[Program Design: Logic; links to Need]**

**5. Wraparound Supports**
**We pair instruction with childcare and transportation stipends.** On-site childcare is available during evening classes, and participants receive [transit passes/$X per week] in transportation support. A Learner Navigator meets with each participant at intake and monthly thereafter to resolve barriers before they lead to dropout. Wraparound services are strongly associated with higher retention in adult education [Source, Year].
*Staffing:* [1.0] FTE Learner Navigator; childcare through [partner/contracted provider]. **[Program Design: Logic, Staffing]**

**Oversight:** A [0.5] FTE Program Director supervises all staff, manages partnerships, and leads quarterly data review. *(Full staffing table in Section 5.)* **[Program Design: Staffing]**

### Evidence Base

Our model draws on established research in adult literacy:

- Structured, explicit reading instruction improves outcomes for adult learners with low literacy [Source, e.g., NIFL/NCES, Year].
- Contextualized instruction tied to work and life goals increases persistence and skill gains [Source, Year].
- Removing logistical barriers such as childcare and transportation reduces dropout, which is a leading cause of program failure in adult education [Source, Year].
- Family literacy programming improves both adult skills and children's reading outcomes [Source, Year].

[Organization]'s own [pilot/prior program] achieved [X]% retention and [X]% level gains in [year] [Internal data], demonstrating that this approach works with Eastside residents. **[Program Design: Logic]**

### Rollout Milestones

| Timeframe | Milestone |
|---|---|
| Months 1–3 | Hire staff, train first [25] tutors, finalize school and childcare partnerships, contact all 120 waitlisted adults |
| Month 4 | Launch Cycle 1 with [3–4] cohorts; waitlisted adults enrolled first |
| Month 8 | Cycle 1 exit assessments; Cycle 2 begins; first quarterly data review |
| Month 12 | Waitlist cleared; [150] adults served; Year 1 evaluation report |
| Months 13–24 | Three cycles per year; refine model based on Year 1 data; expand tutor corps to [50] |

**[Program Design: Timeline]**

---

*≈800 words, excluding tags and table formatting.*

## Phrasing Hooks to Copy

1. "Most literacy programs address skill barriers alone. Ours also removes the participation barriers that cause adults to leave before they can succeed."
2. "Each 16-week cycle provides approximately [96] hours of instruction, enough for most learners to advance one full educational functioning level."
3. "We pair instruction with childcare and transportation stipends, because an adult who cannot get to class cannot learn to read."

## Quick Notes

- **Check the math across sections.** [3–4] cohorts × [12–15] adults × 3 cycles should equal your [150] annual target, after accounting for re-enrollment. Make sure Sections 3, 5, and 8 use the same figures.
- **Note the timeline gap.** Because classes don't launch until Month 4, Year 1 has only about two and a half cycles. Confirm that [150] served in Year 1 is realistic, or describe it as "enrolled" rather than "completed."
- **Build the logic model attachment now.** This section references it, and the same structure will feed directly into Outcomes & Evaluation.

Next up would be Outcomes & Objectives, the 20% section. The pathway above already gives us natural measurement points (intake, exit, 3 and 6 months).

# Outcomes & Objectives

*Inline tags show which rubric points each passage satisfies. Placeholders are in [brackets]. Suggested targets are realistic starting points. Adjust them to match your pilot data.*

---

## Outcomes & Objectives

[Program Name] measures success by change in participants, not by services delivered alone. Our objectives follow the participant pathway: we establish each learner's baseline at intake, measure skill gains at exit (Week 16), and track real-world results at 3 and 6 months. **[Outcomes: Measurable outcomes, Baseline]**

### Outputs vs. Outcomes

| Outputs (what we deliver, per year) | Outcomes (what changes for participants) |
|---|---|
| [150] adults enrolled; 120 waitlisted adults served first | Adults stay enrolled long enough to learn |
| ~[96] instructional hours per cycle, 3 cycles per year | Reading levels rise measurably |
| [150] tutor matches; [12] Family Literacy Nights | Parents read more with their children |
| [150] participants receive childcare/transportation support | Adults gain employment or advance to further training |

**[Outcomes: Measurable outcomes]**

### SMART Objectives

**Objective 1: Persistence.** By the end of each 16-week cycle, **[75]%** of enrolled participants will complete the cycle (attending at least [70]% of instructional hours), up from a baseline of **[X]%** [pilot data/state adult education average, Year]. *Linked to: wraparound supports, Learner Navigator.* **[Outcomes: Measurable, Baseline]**

**Objective 2: Literacy Gains.** By exit, **[60]%** of cycle completers will advance at least one Educational Functioning Level on the [CASAS/TABE] post-test, compared with a baseline of **[X]%** [state adult education measurable skill gain rate, Year]. *Linked to: instruction, tutoring.* **[Outcomes: Measurable, Baseline]**

**Objective 3: Family Engagement.** By exit, **[75]%** of participating parents will report reading with their children at least [3] times per week, up from their intake baseline of **[X]%**. *Linked to: Family Literacy Nights, applied modules.* **[Outcomes: Measurable, Baseline; links to Need]**

**Objective 4: Economic Mobility.** At the 6-month follow-up, **[35]%** of participants who were unemployed or seeking better work at intake will obtain employment, increase hours or wages, or enroll in GED/job training. *Linked to: applied workforce modules, partner referrals.* **[Outcomes: Measurable, Baseline; links to Need]**

**Two-year targets:** [300] enrolled, [225] completers, [135] advancing one or more levels.

### Measurement Tools and Timing

| Tool | Intake | Exit (Wk 16) | 3 Mo | 6 Mo | Collected By |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [CASAS/TABE] assessment | ✓ | ✓ | | | Instructors |
| Attendance records | ongoing | ✓ | | | Instructors |
| Family literacy survey | ✓ | ✓ | | | Learner Navigator |
| Employment/education check-in | ✓ | | ✓ | ✓ | Learner Navigator |

Staff will enter data into [LACES/state adult education database/CRM]. The Program Director will analyze results quarterly and adjust instruction or supports when targets fall behind. *(Full methods in Section 7.)* **[Outcomes: Methods, Baseline]**

---

*≈400 words, excluding tags and tables.*

## Phrasing Hooks to Copy

1. "Every learner's baseline is established at intake, so each gain we report is measured against that individual's own starting point."
2. "By exit, [60]% of completers will advance at least one full Educational Functioning Level, exceeding the state benchmark of [X]%."
3. "We track outcomes for six months after exit, because the real measure of literacy is a job secured, a form completed, or a story read aloud to a child."

## Quick Notes

- **Check the math.** At 150 enrolled, 75% completion gives about 113 completers per year, and 60% of those gives about 68 level gains per year. Use these figures for cost per outcome in the Budget Narrative.
- **Year 1 follow-up timing.** Cycle 1 exits at Month 8, so its 6-month follow-up falls at Month 14. Year 1 reports will show early employment data only. Say so in the evaluation plan so reviewers don't think the data is missing.
- **Post-test timing.** Confirm that your [CASAS/TABE] post-test window fits the publisher's minimum instructional hours. At ~96 hours it should, but cite the guideline.
- **Baselines.** Pilot data is the strongest baseline. Use state averages only as a fallback.

Next is the Evaluation Plan (Section 7). It builds directly on this table, so it should go quickly.

# Evaluation Plan

*Inline tags show which rubric points each passage satisfies. Placeholders are in [brackets].*

---

## Evaluation Plan

### Design

We will use a **pre/post design** that measures each participant against their own intake baseline. We will add **two comparison points**: the state's adult education skill-gain rate for similar learners [State NRS Report, Year] and our own [Year] pilot cohort. A randomized design would require withholding services from adults who have already waited six months, which we consider unethical. Benchmark comparison gives reviewers meaningful context without denying anyone a seat. **[Outcomes: Methods, Baseline]**

### Data Collection

Data collection follows the Outcomes table (Section 6). We use standardized [CASAS/TABE] assessments at intake and exit, attendance records throughout, a family literacy survey at intake and exit, and employment/education check-ins at intake, 3 months, and 6 months. Learners can complete follow-ups by phone, text, or in person, with staff reading the questions aloud. **[Outcomes: Methods, Measurable outcomes]**

### Roles and Qualifications

- **Instructors** (certified in [CASAS/TABE] administration) conduct assessments and record attendance.
- **Learner Navigator** administers surveys and follow-ups.
- **Program Director** ([X] years of adult education data management) analyzes data quarterly.
- **[Optional: External evaluator, University/Firm]** validates findings and authors the annual report.

**[Outcomes: Methods; Capacity]**

### Data Management and Privacy

Participants give informed consent at intake, read aloud in plain language. Data is stored in [LACES/CRM] with role-based access and encryption. Analysis files use ID numbers, not names, and results are reported only in aggregate. No individual data is shared with partners without written consent. **[Outcomes: Methods]**

### Reporting and Continuous Improvement

| Audience | Frequency | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Staff | Monthly | Attendance and retention dashboard |
| Leadership and partners | Quarterly | Progress toward objectives, barriers, adjustments |
| Funder | [Semiannual/Annual] | Full outcomes report against targets |

If a cohort falls more than [10] points below a target, staff will review the data within two weeks and adjust instruction, scheduling, or supports. Each adjustment will be documented in quarterly reports. **[Outcomes: Methods; Program Design: Logic]**

### Sample Size and Limitations

About [113] completers per year is enough to detect a 15-point difference from the state benchmark (for example, 60% vs. 45%) with about 80% power. Detecting that difference requires roughly 85 completers. Three limitations apply:

- The design does not use a control group, so the results show association, not causation.
- Follow-up response rates may fall to [50–60]%. We will report response rates alongside results.
- Year 1 will include only early 6-month data, because the first 6-month follow-up falls in Month 14.

**[Outcomes: Methods, Measurable outcomes]**

---

*≈400 words, excluding tags and table.*

## Suggested Survey Items

1. **Family engagement:** "In the past week, how many days did you read or look at books with your child?" *(0 / 1–2 / 3–4 / 5–7 days)*
2. **Family engagement:** "How confident do you feel helping your child with schoolwork?" *(Not at all / A little / Somewhat / Very)*
3. **Employment:** "Since finishing the program, have any of these happened? (Check all)" *(Got a job / More hours or pay / Started GED or training / None yet)*

## Quick Notes

- **Budget an external evaluator if you can.** External evaluation typically costs [5–10]% of the program budget and strengthens credibility. Name it in the Budget Narrative.
- **Plan for follow-up attrition.** Collect two contact methods at intake and offer a small incentive (for example, a [$10] gift card) to improve response rates.

Next is the Budget Narrative (15%), where we can use the per-participant and per-outcome math from Section 6.

Nice work. You've now drafted the sections that carry **80% of the score**:

- ✅ Statement of Need
- ✅ Target Population
- ✅ Program Design & Activities
- ✅ Outcomes & Objectives
- ✅ Evaluation Plan

**Still to go:** Budget Narrative (15%), Organizational Capacity and Sustainability (5%), and the Executive Summary, which is easiest to write last.

When you're ready for the Budget Narrative, it will go faster if you have these on hand:

- Total request amount and grant period
- Salaries or hourly rates for each role (Instructors, Learner Navigator, Volunteer Coordinator, Program Director)
- Fringe rate and indirect rate
- Childcare and transportation stipend costs
- Assessment, curriculum, and materials costs
- External evaluator estimate, if you're including one
- Any in-kind or matched funds

Rough numbers or placeholders are fine. Just say the word whenever you want to keep going, whether that's now or after some rest.
